This project examines how the presentation of human–AI collaboration, scientific uncertainty, and supporting explanations shapes public acceptance of AI chatbots for health misinformation correction. Guided by the Human–AI Interaction framework grounded in the Theory of Interactive Media Effects (HAII–TIME), the study investigates whether these features independently and jointly influence trust in a chatbot, attitudes toward using it to correct health misinformation, and intentions to use it for this purpose. The study employed a 3 × 2 × 2 between-subjects online experiment with a final analytical sample of 424 participants in China. Participants were randomly assigned to one of 12 conditions and viewed a simulated chatbot conversation addressing the false claim that insulin injections are addictive. Human–AI collaboration was described as human-dominated, with experts leading the evaluation and AI assisting; AI-dominated, with AI leading and experts verifying; or AI-only, without human involvement. Correction uncertainty varied according to whether the accompanying notice described the scientific evidence as broadly consistent or unresolved. Correction transparency varied according to whether the chatbot disclosed supporting reasons and sources. Analyses examined the main and interaction effects of these features while accounting for demographic characteristics, AI literacy, eHealth literacy, and perceived risks of AI hallucinations.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Road accidents remain a critical public safety issue, where detection often depends on witnesses calling authorities, leading to delays of several minutes before police and ambulances are dispatched. This study presents CrashSenseAI (CSAI), an Edge artificial intelligence (Edge AI) accident detection and notification system built on You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) and YOLOv12 models. Using a labeled dataset of accident and non-accident images, we trained Nano, Small, and Medium variants with batch sizes of 16 and 32 to evaluate accuracy–latency trade-offs. Results show YOLOv12n achieved the lowest inference latency (3.6–3.7 ms) with high precision (0.89), while YOLOv8s provided the best balance of accuracy and efficiency (Recall 0.85, Precision 0.90, mean average precision (mAP) at an Intersection over Union threshold of 0.5 (mAP@0.5 = 0.89) and mAP@0.5–0.95 = 0.70) at 4.8–5.0 ms. Larger variants improved mAP@0.5 scores (up to 0.90) but incurred higher latency (11–14 ms). CSAI captures timestamped frames with latitude and longitude, automatically notifying police, ambulances, and nearby hospitals to speed response and scene clearance, reduce traffic congestion, and improve victim survival during the golden hour. By combining real-time detection, geolocation, evidence generation, and automated alerting, CSAI demonstrates practical scalability for AI-driven intelligent transportation and road safety applications.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: Abstract Pediatric and adult cancers diverge profoundly in their molecular architecture, yet whether these differences extend to genome-scale genetic dependencies remains poorly characterized, with prior studies examining single subtypes or individual algorithms rather than a systematic, interpretable comparison. To address this gap, we tested whether Clustered Regularly Interspaced Short Palindromic Repeats (CRISPR)-Cas9 loss-of-function dependency profiles can discriminate pediatric from adult cancer cell lines, and applied explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to identify the genes driving this distinction. Chronos-normalized CRISPR GeneEffect scores for 18,531 genes across 1208 cell lines (242 pediatric, 966 adult) were analyzed; class imbalance was corrected with the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) within each training fold, differentially dependent genes were identified by Mann-Whitney U tests with Benjamini-Hochberg False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction, and 200 features were retained by SelectKBest. Eleven classifiers were benchmarked under 5-fold cross-validation across 11 metrics, and predictions were interpreted with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations (LIME) In this first (to our knowledge) genome-scale, multi-classifier comparison Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM) achieved the best discrimination (Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic Curve [ROC-AUC] = 0.909, accuracy = 88.7%, Matthews Correlation Coefficient [MCC] = 0.632, Brier score = 0.089), with the leading ensemble and margin-based models reaching ROC-AUC values near 0.90. Among 3602 differentially dependent genes (FDR < 0.05), Integrin-Linked Kinase (ILK), Talin-1 (TLN1), and Aurora Kinase A (AURKA) showed greater dependency in pediatric lines, whereas Glutathione Peroxidase 4 (GPX4) and Insulin-like Growth Factor 2 messenger RNA-Binding Protein 1 (IGF2BP1) were comparatively more essential in adult lines. SHAP highlighted CHMP4B, IGF2BP1, GPX4, and LDB1, and the representative true-positive LIME case emphasized IGF2BP1, PAQR6, and CDS2. By exposing dependencies that adult-centric precision-oncology programs overlook, this work provides a framework for age-specific target discovery and prioritizes the pediatric-enriched ILK–TLN1 mechanotransduction axis for experimental validation.

Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare poses significant challenges for evaluation due to algorithmic complexity and evolving performance. Existing evidence generation guidelines, primarily designed for static medical technologies, may inadequately address the unique characteristics of generative AI. Here, we conducted a comparative analysis of evidence generation guidelines from six countries, examining recommendations for efficacy and effectiveness evaluations, health economic evaluations, social and equity evaluations, and uncertainty management for AI technologies. Across 56 documents, we found a consistent preference for randomised controlled trials and cost-effectiveness analyses, alongside emerging acceptance of alternative study designs and real-world evidence to accommodate the evolving nature of AI technologies. However, current frameworks lack specific guidance for the stochastic, non-deterministic, and adaptive learning properties of generative AI technologies. Moving forward, evidence generation guidelines require methodological and conceptual adaptations in order to improve the value assessment for generative AI technologies.
topics: Health Systems, Economic Evaluations, Quality of Life
Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract Surface ligand-modified nanoparticles (SMNPs), which immobilize surface ligands on nanoscale scaffolds, represent important nanomaterials for diverse applications. While surface ligands critically dictate the functions of SMNPs, their systematic discovery remains elusive. The major challenge in using artificial intelligence to predict and screen effective surface ligands and SMNPs across extensive chemical space is the scarcity of high-quality, standardized data sets. This impedes SMNP nanotechnology and leaves an enormous functional landscape largely unmapped. For antibacterial gold nanoparticles, available surface-ligand data sets are extremely sparse (<102), whereas public small-molecule libraries exceed 1010 entries. Here, we introduce a cross-scale (from small molecules to nanoparticles) transfer-cascade learning framework, called TRADE, that transforms the structural–activity patterns of molecular antibiotics into predictive principles for the surface ligands of nanoparticle antibiotics. Within TRADE, we chemically deconstruct molecular antibiotics into conserved scaffolds and variable substituents for transfer learning and combine a multitier, coarse-to-fine cascade to narrow the search space. We identify a new class of 24 surface ligands with high predicted antibacterial efficacy for decorating gold nanoparticles across over 9 million molecules. The leading auricidin inhibits bacterial peptidoglycan biosynthesis and demonstrates potent antimicrobial activity against multidrug-resistant pathogens, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus and vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus faecium, with minimum inhibitory concentrations as low as 0.5–1 μg/mL. Across multiple animal infection models, auricidin exhibits exceptional therapeutic efficacy and robustness, superior to vancomycin, minimal toxicity, and low susceptibility to resistance evolution. This work proposes an intelligent strategy for discovering new functional nanoscale entities by integrating cross-domain transfer and cascade learning.

Machine Learning Services help enterprises turn data into actionable intelligence through predictive models, intelligent automation, personalization, and real-time decision-making. From ML consulting and custom model development to MLOps, deployment, and optimization, these services support the complete machine learning lifecycle.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Customer retention has become increasingly important for organizations operating in highly competitive service industries. In the local non-alcoholic beverage sector, businesses continuously seek strategies that can strengthen customer relationships and encourage long-term patronage. Despite the recognized importance of customer satisfaction and customer engagement, limited studies have examined how these variables collectively influence customer retention within local beverage enterprises. Guided by Expectancy Disconfirmation Theory, the Consumers' Online Brand-Related Activities Framework, and Service-Profit Chain Theory, this study examined customer satisfaction, customer engagement, and customer retention intent among customers of selected local non-alcoholic beverage chains in Valenzuela City. The study further investigated demographic differences, examined the relationships among the variables, evaluated the mediating role of customer engagement, and developed a Customer Engagement-Satisfaction-Retention Framework. Findings revealed that respondents generally demonstrated favorable levels of customer engagement, customer satisfaction, and customer retention intent. Product quality emerged as the most influential component of customer satisfaction, while cognitive engagement was the strongest dimension of customer engagement. The results further showed that customer satisfaction significantly influences customer engagement and customer retention intent. Customer engagement likewise significantly affects customer retention intent and serves as an important mechanism through which satisfaction translates into stronger retention-related behaviors. The proposed Customer Engagement-Satisfaction-Retention Framework highlights the importance of integrating service excellence, customer engagement initiatives, and customer satisfaction strategies to achieve sustainable customer loyalty and long-term business success. The findings contribute to customer relationship management literature and provide practical insights for local beverage enterprises seeking to improve competitiveness and customer retention.

Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a pivotal advancement in textile systems, integrating intelligent sensing, wearable computing, IoT, and machine learning applications on smart fabrics for real-time monitoring of object behavior through predictive analytics. The primary areas of application identified in the investigation include healthcare, industrial safety, sports and fitness. Emerging domains represent; AI-enhanced wearable fabrics are perpetually evolving for ongoing patient surveillance and preventive health measures. The most significant security risk identified during this analysis is data breaches, closely followed by limited system access, adversarial AI assaults and denial of service attacks. Privacy-preserving technologies have emerged as a significant domain, with encryption along with blockchain, edge computing, and federated learning. This meta-analysis offers insights regarding contemporary research trends and obstacles in cybersecurity which will assist researchers in creating secure and sustainable AI-integrated wearable textile systems.

Digital supply chains face cybersecurity threats from interconnectedness and IoT devices. Real-time tracking increases risks in cyber-physical systems with vulnerable endpoints. Blockchain-IoT integration creates vulnerabilities through weak security protocols. Risk frameworks like ISO 31000 and NIST SP 800-30 guide risk identification and treatment. AI enables anomaly detection, while blockchain provides immutable records. Regulatory compliance with CCPA, GDPR, and ISO 28000 ensures data privacy. Industry 5.0 emphasizes human-AI collaboration for resilience. Future developments include AI analytics and IoT security through lightweight cryptography. Integrating cybersecurity with sustainability will support resilient supply chains. Multidisciplinary collaboration and adaptive governance address risks in value-driven networks.
topics: Supply Chain Resilience and Risk Management

documents.abstract: This project contains the de-identified data and supporting documentation for the study “How Should AI Voice Guides Explain Paintings? An Experimental Study of Guidance Strategy and Voice Persona Using Chinese Landscape Paintings.” The study used a Unity-based virtual gallery featuring six Chinese landscape paintings. A 3 × 2 within-subjects experiment with 21 university students compared three guidance strategies—Minimal Prompt, Standard Introduction, and Active Inquiry—and two voice personas—Warm Young Female Guide and Calm Senior Male Guide. The outcomes included user engagement, subjective task load, human–AI trust, and immediate knowledge retention. The shared files include participant-level observations across the experimental conditions, variable definitions, scoring procedures, and documentation of missing or invalid knowledge-test records. These materials support the reproduction of the statistical analyses, tables, and figures reported in the manuscript. Participants are represented by anonymous identifiers, and directly identifying information is excluded.

As claims about recursive self-improvement (RSI) and artificial general intelligence (AGI) proliferate, we ask a simple question: do frontier AI models have a sense of data, i.e., can they reliably select the right data for training? We introduce DataSense-Bench to study this capability through the fundamental problem of data selection and performance forecasting in machine learning. We ask AI agents to select and rank candidate training subsets that can be used to fine-tune a small LLM model. Agents are allowed to inspect the data, write and execute analysis code, and run model forward passes, but can not train the model or access the actual evaluation tasks. We then fine-tune the base model on each selected subset and evaluate its post-training performance under a standardized protocol. We instantiate the benchmark in terminal problem solving and tool use, selecting trajectories from OpenThoughts-Agent and EnvScaler and evaluating on TBLite and BFCL, respectively. We then evaluate the agents along two complementary dimensions: the post-training performance of the top-ranked subset, reflecting the ability to identify high-value training data, and ranking accuracy, reflecting the ability to predict the relative performance of the selected subsets. In our experiments, selection gains over random selection are limited; agents do not reliably rank their selected groups, and ranking ability does not hold consistently across tasks: Astra identifies the best group in all three tool-use runs but in only one of three terminal runs. Analysis of execution traces on both tasks shows that agents often use similar data signals while interpreting their training value differently.

Data video is a media form that integrates data visualization with video narrative, widely adopted in news reporting and business analysis. Compared with general video understanding, data video understanding places greater emphasis on accurately reading data from animated charts, integrating evidence across charts and time, and understanding how narrative organization and visual design communicate information. Yet existing benchmarks target either general videos or static charts, and data video understanding has not been systematically evaluated. We present DataVista, the first benchmark for data video understanding, containing 961 real-world data videos and 6,775 evaluation questions organized under a three-level progressive capability framework (data perception, temporal reasoning, narrative understanding) with 10 fine-grained question types across five topic domains. Systematic evaluation of 19 mainstream MLLMs shows that the best-performing model, Gemini-3.1-Pro, achieves 70.0% overall accuracy, still far below human expert performance, with models performing worst on Causal Reasoning and Narrative Structure. Increasing frame counts and adding subtitles mainly benefit data perception and temporal reasoning, with limited gains in narrative understanding. Further analysis of model responses identifies typical failure modes in chart reading, evidence judgment, and instruction understanding. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/HKUSTDial/DataVista.

This chapter examines decentralized education ecosystems by integrating blockchain, artificial intelligence, and the metaverse for next-generation learning. It explains how blockchain can provide trust, secure credentials, learner-owned records, and verifiable micro-certifications, while AI supports personalization, adaptive learning, intelligent tutoring, analytics, and competency-based assessment. The metaverse adds immersive classrooms, simulations, digital campuses, and experiential skill development. The chapter argues that these technologies can transform education from institution-centered systems to learner-centered, portable, flexible, and lifelong learning ecosystems. It also discusses challenges such as data privacy, algorithmic bias, digital inequality, credential fraud, platform control, metaverse safety, and quality assurance.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly act as agents with little human oversight, so potential mistakes they make can go unnoticed. Users then depend on the model to report what went wrong. An honest model discloses its mistakes, while a deceptive one conceals them. However, it is unclear how current LLMs behave in such situations. In this study, we prefill LLM trajectories with synthetic mistakes. The trajectories resemble real deployments in chat and agentic settings. Models fail to disclose their mistake in 36.4% of chat and 67.1% of agentic rollouts. In 2.4% and 5.3% of rollouts, respectively, they are aware of the mistake in their chain of thought but still deceptively conceal it. Rates vary by model: for instance, Gemini 3.5 Flash knowingly conceals mistakes in up to 19.9% of agentic rollouts. In 11.9% of chat and 51.8% of agentic rollouts, models show no awareness of mistakes, even though they reliably spot them when reviewing the same transcript as an outside observer. Our results show that, as agents take on more tasks with less oversight, users cannot rely on them to self-report possible mistakes. Developers should instead use independent monitors that review agent trajectories, or specifically train models to check their past actions and disclose what they find.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The modern workplace is an intricate emotional ecosystem where human behavior, psychological well-being, and professional performance are deeply intertwined. This chapter explores the transformative convergence of artificial intelligence and emotional intelligence as a comprehensive framework for understanding, predicting, and supporting human behavior across professional contexts. Artificial intelligence is examined as an external cognitive companion that augments human decision-making and extends the practical reach of emotional intelligence into environments where direct human intervention is limited. Through natural language processing and computer vision, AI systems decode the emotional signals embedded in language, facial expression, and behavioral patterns, enabling meaningful prediction of workforce dynamics. Emotional intelligence is explored across three applied pillars — emotional appraisal, self-regulation, and purposeful emotional utilization — each carrying direct implications for leadership, collaboration, and organizational health.

The current high rate of adoption of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has led to a sense of urgency in the need to come up with immediate faculty-level literacy development. The idea of prompt literacy described in this chapter is a conceptual extension of AI literacy, focusing on the skill of developing effective prompts to achieve meaningful results in teaching, learning and assessment. It explores the current gaps in faculty preparedness and points to the absence of systematic institutional strategies to promote this new competency. The chapter also suggests faculty developmental strategies that are based on experiential learning, ethical awareness and continuous skill improvement. It also gives a detailed institutional framework to inform the systematic incorporation of prompt literacy into the faculty development programs. The chapter, with its focus on pedagogical and organizational aspects, will also help create a sustainable, responsible and context-sensitive implementation of AI in higher education.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: As leading LLMs improve on capability evaluations, their limitations in producing creative outputs on design tasks remain insufficiently characterised. Our work introduces Design Creativity Bench, a benchmark that evaluates diversity and appropriateness in UI designs. It measures distinctiveness among models on the same prompt (originality), how much a model's designs change between two prompts for the same UI goal in different product domains (creative range), and the share of a brief's acceptance criteria each design meets (appropriateness). Originality is 0.592 for same-prompt design pairs from different models (95% CI [0.582, 0.602]), far below the 0.764 for same-prompt human-model pairs (95% CI [0.751, 0.778]). Creative range is 0.581 across models (95% CI [0.567, 0.597]), against 0.902 for human designs (95% CI [0.884, 0.919]). Appropriateness is above 90% for every model, and the best model reaches 99.2%, slightly above the 98.0% for human designs. Our work shows that the default output of LLMs, though generally appropriate, is substantially more repetitive than the human baseline. This calls for strong measures to address the issue.

Healthcare monitoring is an important area where technology can significantly improve the quality, accessibility, and efficiency of medical services. Traditional healthcare systems mainly depend on periodic hospital visits and manual monitoring of patients, which may not provide continuous information about a patient's health condition. The combination of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and the Internet of Things (IoT) provides an effective solution for continuous and intelligent healthcare monitoring. In an AI-based smart healthcare monitoring system, IoT sensors are used to collect real-time physiological information such as heart rate, body temperature, blood oxygen saturation, blood pressure, and other health-related parameters. The collected data is transmitted through an IoT communication network to a cloud or processing platform. AI and machine learning techniques can then analyze the collected data, identify abnormal patterns, and support early detection of potential health problems. The proposed system provides continuous monitoring, automatic data analysis, alerts, and remote access to health information. This reduces the need for frequent manual observation and helps healthcare professionals make informed decisions based on real-time patient information. The system can be particularly useful for elderly people, patients requiring continuous observation, individuals with chronic health conditions, and remote healthcare environments. The integration of AI, IoT sensors, cloud computing, and mobile applications creates a smart healthcare environment that improves monitoring efficiency and supports timely medical intervention

Artificial intelligence (AI) is now part of everyday academic work in higher education, including feedback. However, AI feedback does not automatically lead to learning. It can help students rethink a concept, improve a draft, and notice gaps in their work, but it can also create a false sense of progress when students accept suggestions without understanding them. This Perspective article argues that responsible AI feedback depends on faculty readiness and students’ evaluative judgement. Readiness is not mainly technical. It involves pedagogical judgement: knowing how to design tasks in which students work with feedback, compare it with evidence, revise with purpose, explain their choices, and remain responsible for the final submission. The article focuses on generative AI feedback and uses metacognitive calibration as a central concept. Calibration refers to the relationship between students’ confidence or self-judgement and independently evaluated evidence of performance. Evaluative judgement concerns students’ capacity to judge the quality and relevance of feedback and work, whereas calibration concerns the accuracy of their judgements relative to independently evaluated performance evidence. The article shows how ideas from feedback literacy, evaluative judgement, and self-regulated learning need to be adapted when feedback comes from systems whose accuracy and educational value cannot be assumed. It proposes a conceptual responsible AI feedback design cycle linked to assessment integrity, university policy, and faculty development. Although the cycle requires empirical testing, it offers a practical way to support reflection, calibrated judgement, and accountability without replacing students’ thinking.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This study examines how information source type, information accuracy, information type, and presentation modality shape perceived source credibility in generative AI settings. A four-way factorial experiment (N = 960) revealed that information accuracy was the dominant determinant of source credibility, while source type (human, AI) and presentation modality (text, video) produced no significant effects. The credibility penalty for factual inaccuracy was nearly four times larger than the penalty for counter-attitudinal opinion content, consistent with Expectancy Violations Theory: higher baseline accuracy expectations in verifiable domains amplify the credibility penalty for error. A significant three-way interaction further showed that human sources incurred larger penalties for factual errors than AI sources, suggesting that individuals apply unequal accuracy standards depending on source identity. The credibility consequences of accuracy violations are thus context-dependent, varying by information type and source identity. These findings offer theoretical and practical insights for AI literacy education and generative AI design.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The integration of three-dimensional (3D) and augmented reality (AR) technologies into anatomy education facilitates broader access to anatomical content and enhances learner motivation and cognitive engagement by enabling interactive, spatially rich exploration of complex structures. However, high costs, technical complexity, and restricted access to specialized imaging equipment and software often hinder adoption of these digital anatomy tools. This study aimed to develop a smartphone-LiDAR-assisted photogrammetry workflow for generating low-cost, accessible and realistic 3D models for anatomy education. A canine femur was digitized following a streamlined workflow that included specimen preparation, LIDAR-assisted image acquisition using a smartphone, photogrammetric reconstruction, and hosting of the resulting model in 3D web and AR format in an online learning management system platform called Clon Digital. The anatomical plausibility of the generated model was assessed through a rubric-based expert review conducted by seven independent veterinary anatomy lecturers, focusing on morphology, anatomical landmarks, surface detail, and overall reconstruction quality. Subsequently, the educational usability and user experience of the model was analyzed through a multidimensional perception survey completed by veterinary students and lecturers (n = 141). The survey focused on anatomical fidelity, educational value, self-learning potential, user interface, and engagement. Participants reported high satisfaction across all domains while identifying minor technical limitations. These findings indicate that smartphone-based LiDAR-assisted photogrammetry can generate and distribute 3D-AR models using an accessible workflow for educational use. This workflow offers an ethical, cost-effective, and scalable complement that supports the integration of immersive digital anatomy resources in anatomical education.

The thesis proposes a didactic model for organizing practical classes in specialized subjects based on Smart Agriculture technologies at higher agricultural education institutions. The model is based on the sequence “Question — Data — Analysis — Decision — Presentation — Reflection.” Students work with real or simulated agrotechnological data using IoT sensors, GIS, digital monitoring, remote sensing, and artificial intelligence tools. This approach is aimed at connecting theoretical knowledge with practical tasks, developing data literacy, and fostering skills for making informed professional decisions.

. This paper examines the didactic potential of meta-technologies for developing the innovative competence of higher education teaching staff. Particular attention is paid to cloud services, big data, artificial intelligence, no-code environments and immersive tools. The paper discusses the pedagogical criteria for selecting technologies, a step-by-step procedure for developing digital learning resources, and assessment approaches that focus on meaningful educational outcomes rather than the mere frequency of technology use.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: Prompt learning is a popular method for adapting foundation models, but learned prompts are typically task-specific and fail to generalize to new classes, domains, or compositions of tasks. In this paper, we introduce a Diffusion Meta-Prompt (DMP) model , a framework that models the distribution of learned prompts using diffusion models. Given a repository of previously learned prompts, DMP is trained and sampled without access to the original task examples or task losses, and synthesizes new prompts conditioned on natural language task descriptions. To improve the sampling stability, we introduce a test-time steering strategy for DMP, which uses the best training-selected prompt in the repository as a latent anchor during diffusion sampling, without retraining the DMP or accessing test classes. DMP improves generalization across classification, retrieval and text-to-image generation tasks, supports concept composition and negative prompting without explicit training. It reduces storage and inference costs by over 90% compared to prompt retrieval methods. For composite classification, DMP achieves upto 2.0% average gain over prior meta-learning methods across 55 pairs of datasets with gains as high as 8.5% on specific pairs such as Eurosat and Flowers. DMP also enhances cross-task generalization with ~2-9% improvement for hierarchical classification task. We further provide a theoretical guarantee bounding the expected task loss of prompts sampled from a DMP. Code is available: https://github.com/DeepakSridhar/dmp

This article argues that as digitalisation and artificial intelligence become increasingly embedded in design practice, the preservation of cultural memory is shifting from physical spaces to digital environments structured by data and algorithms. While these technological transformations open up new possibilities for design methods and the transmission of cultural memory, they also introduce challenges: algorithm-driven rationality risks reducing the depth of human emotions and homogenising diverse cultural memories. Drawing on the theory of Archives of Feelings and visual culture studies, and adopting the concept of historical empathy proposed as a framework, this study analyses three key dimensions of cultural memory as mediated through visual design: social collective memory, marginalised group memory and human–AI collaborative memory. It further explores how visual design can negotiate between technological rationality and humanistic care, ensuring that Digital Archives of Feelings sustain diverse cultural memories while preserving emotional depth.

The widespread use of smartphones and electronic devices has raised concerns about their impact on hand and wrist health. This scoping review synthesised current evidence on musculoskeletal and soft-tissue disorders associated with device use. Thirty-two studies were included, examining smartphones, computers and other digital tools. Smartphones were primarily linked to De Quervain's tenosynovitis and flexor pollicis longus tendinopathy, while computers and visual display units were associated with carpal tunnel syndrome and repetitive strain injuries. Key risk factors included repetitive thumb movements, prolonged static wrist postures and extended daily exposure. Biomechanical studies confirmed increased joint loading and muscle activity during intensive use. Preventive strategies - such as limiting usage time, improving ergonomics, alternating hands and incorporating regular breaks - showed potential benefits, particularly when combined with user education. Most included studies were cross-sectional, limiting causal inference and highlighting the need for longitudinal research.

Technological advancements are reshaping organizational structures, employee roles, and workplace interactions, making work environments increasingly digital, data-driven, and collaborative. The acceleration of digital transformation during the COVID-19 pandemic further reinforced the adoption of remote work models and digital collaboration platforms, highlighting growing importance of digital capabilities, adaptability, and digital well-being. In this evolving landscape, organizations are recognizing that digital transformation extends beyond technological investments to include human-centered approaches that prioritize employee experience. Consequently, the concept of Digital Employee Experience (DEX) has emerged as a critical dimension of modern workplaces, referring to employees' overall interactions with digital tools, systems, and environments throughout the employment lifecycle.This chapter proposes a framework that integrates AI-enabled interventions with DEX to examine their influence on employee well-being, engagement, and retention in digitally transforming workplaces.

Introduction The advent of generative AI has reduced costs, scaled up operations, and made it more difficult to identify disinformation and manipulated content, leading to new governance and security challenges in Africa. This paper analyses the nexus among the manipulation of digital information, governments’ readiness to adopt AI, digital connectivity, and security outcomes in Africa’s five most populous countries, namely Nigeria, South Africa, Egypt, Ethiopia, and the Democratic Republic of Congo, for the period from 2023 to 2026. The research attempts to fill a gap in the existing literature by addressing the lack of empirical research on the relationship between digital information manipulation and government AI readiness, and on its consequences for security issues in Africa. Methods The paper draws on the theoretical frameworks of Social Learning Theory and Routine Activity Theory and uses seven credible datasets, including ACLED, UCDP/PRIO, V-Dem, GSMA, ITU, the Oxford Insights Government AI Readiness Index, and Afrobarometer, to construct a country-year panel. Correlation analyses were conducted to test three hypotheses regarding the relationship among digital manipulation, digital connectivity, institutional readiness for AI adoption, and conflict fatalities. It utilises a verified multisource panel dataset spanning five countries and operationalises AI readiness as an institutional capability distinct from digital exposure. Results Digital manipulation was found to have a weak positive correlation with fatalities ( r = 0.23), a moderate negative correlation with digital connectivity ( r = −0.56), and a weak negative correlation with institutional readiness to adopt AI ( r = −0.42). These findings show that correlations between digital exposure and security consequences may be distorted by underlying conflict contexts. Discussion It can therefore be deduced that although digital manipulation is becoming an emerging security challenge, conflict and other structures are more significant predictors of security outcomes. This study offers an initial cross-national empirical assessment of AI-related security vulnerabilities in Africa and calls for stronger AI governance and longitudinal, event-level research.

The article examines the essence of digital leadership in outsourcing IT companies amid the structural transformation of the global technology services market. It is substantiated that the rapid advancement of artificial intelligence, cloud technologies, digital platforms, and agentic systems is reshaping the traditional determinants of IT companies' competitiveness, shifting the emphasis from the cost of human resources towards management's capacity to integrate digital technologies into business processes and to ensure their economic effectiveness. Contemporary scholarly approaches to interpreting digital leadership are analyzed, the findings of Ukrainian and foreign researchers are synthesized, and the place of digital leadership within the system of enterprise digital transformation is defined. The article explores the development trends of the global IT services market. It analyses the practices of leading international outsourcing companies regarding the adoption of artificial intelligence, the development of proprietary digital platforms, the enhancement of employees' digital competencies, and the use of AI agents in corporate governance. It is established that digital leadership is acquiring the features of a measurable economic category, since its effectiveness is assessed through the volume of orders and revenues generated by digital solutions, the productivity of managerial processes, the reduction of operating costs, and the speed of managerial decision-making. Particular attention is devoted to the current state of digital leadership among Ukrainian outsourcing IT companies. It is revealed that despite renewed positive dynamics in computer services exports and the active use of artificial intelligence tools by IT professionals, a substantial gap persists between the individual application of digital technologies and their systemic integration into corporate governance. It is argued that bridging this gap requires cultivating digital leadership as a comprehensive managerial competence to redesign business processes, deploy agentic technologies, develop employees' digital competencies, and safeguard human control over critical managerial decisions. It is concluded that digital leadership is one of the key factors ensuring the long-term competitiveness of outsourcing IT companies amid the transformation of the global technology services market.

Digital marketing has evolved from a supplementary channel of promotion into the dominant mode through which brands identify, reach, and build relationships with consumers. Since early reviews of the field characterized digital marketing primarily as the use of electronic channels – search, email, and display advertising – to connect with customers, the discipline has been reshaped by two largely unanticipated forces: the mainstreaming of artificial intelligence in campaign personalization and targeting, and a parallel, intensifying shift toward privacy-first data practices driven by regulation, platform policy, and consumer expectation. This paper synthesizes the conceptual foundations of digital marketing with current evidence on these two forces to develop an integrated conceptual framework linking digital marketing channels, AI-enabled personalization, consumer engagement and trust, and business outcomes, with privacy regulation and consumer data trust positioned as a critical moderating condition rather than a peripheral compliance concern. Drawing on recent industry and academic evidence, the paper finds that while AI-driven personalization now touches nearly every stage of the marketing funnel and delivers measurable performance gains, its effectiveness is increasingly conditional on brand’s ability to earn and retain consumer trust in an environment of tightening data-privacy constraints. The paper discusses illustrative applications of the framework, outlines managerial implications for structuring digital marketing strategy in this environment, and identifies directions for future empirical research.

Artificial intelligence increasingly mediates how citizens access information, making digital media literacy a condition for informed participation. This exploratory study conceptualizes a comfort–competence gap, whereby students report confidence and ease in using AI tools but a weaker capacity to evaluate what those tools produce, and examines it among 300 university students in the United Arab Emirates. The gap is advanced provisionally, and all measures are self-reported perceptions rather than demonstrated performance. Cross-sectional questionnaire data (twelve four-point ordinal items) were analyzed with ordinal-appropriate methods. Students generally reported greater confidence and comfort in using AI than capacity to evaluate it critically. Every operational item mean (2.51–2.55) exceeded every critical item mean (2.39–2.44), and the within-person contrast between the composite indices was small but statistically significant (difference = 0.12, p = 0.027, dz = 0.13), a pattern shown by 44.7% of individuals. No item-level contrast reached significance and 36.0% showed the reverse pattern, so the difference is read as an exploratory tendency rather than evidence of a general gap. The contrast is also sensitive to the composition of the operational index: with comfort removed, it retains its direction, but not conventional significance (p = 0.056). Digital confidence was the only correlate of comfort in AI-mediated communication (ρ = 0.131; OR = 1.29), a weak association in a model with minimal explanatory power (McFadden pseudo-R2 = 0.012); communication competence and demographic characteristics showed no detectable associations, and parallel analysis retained no factors. Interpreted cautiously, the pattern bears on responsible AI use, since comfort unmatched by evaluative capacity is a weak basis for human oversight. The study’s clearest contribution is methodological: single-item self-report batteries can profile levels and detect aggregate differences, but they cannot show whether AI literacy is one capacity or several, cannot separate real capability from what respondents are willing to claim, and cannot support strong conclusions from null results. It therefore specifies the multi-item and performance-based measurement agenda a confirmatory test would require.

This article examines the distinctive characteristics of the digital generation, its level of proficiency in using information and communication technologies (ICT), and the challenges of adapting the modern education system to the needs of a new generation and the demands of the digital age. Digitalization processes are significantly transforming educational content, teaching methods, and instructional tools, necessitating the adoption of innovative pedagogical approaches. The article also explores the development of digital competencies, the effective use of distance and blended learning opportunities, and the role of artificial intelligence and emerging educational technologies in the teaching and learning process. Furthermore, it highlights the significance of digital transformation in improving the quality of education and preparing highly qualified, competitive professionals equipped to meet the demands of an increasingly digital and knowledge-driven society.
topics: Innovations in Education and Learning Technologies

documents.abstract: The article examines digitalization as a factor transforming the exercise of public authority and defines its constitutional and legal significance for public administration, mechanisms of popular sovereignty, and the judiciary. It argues that the current stage of digital transformation goes beyond merely converting established procedures into electronic formats; digital systems are increasingly integrated into processes of information processing, the making of legally significant decisions, and the exercise of public authority. The article analyzes the legal framework for the provision of electronic public services and the operation of public electronic registers, electronic petitions, public consultations, and the Unified Judicial Information and Telecommunication System. Particular attention is paid to the permissible limits of algorithmic administrative discretion, digital inclusion, voter information autonomy, and the use of artificial intelligence systems in judicial proceedings. The author proposes viewing the digitalization of public authority through the interconnection of infrastructural, procedural, participatory, and guarantee-related dimensions. It is argued that the guarantee-related dimension is cross-cutting, encompassing requirements for legality, legal certainty, transparency, proportionality, equality, data protection, individual accountability, judicial oversight, and effective legal protection. The article formulates the principle of the non-loss of constitutional guarantees resulting from digital transformation, according to which a change in the technological form of exercising a governmental function cannot lead to a narrowing of the scope of an individual's legal protection. The methodological basis comprises systemic, formal-legal, structural-functional, comparative-legal, and axiological methods. It is concluded that digital constitutionalism should be viewed as an evolution of classical constitutionalism aimed at establishing legal limits on the use of technology within the sphere of public authority, ensuring meaningful human control, and preserving the human-centric nature of constitutional regulation.

With the global aging population, research on exergames for healthy aging has grown. Yet the use of theories, models, and frameworks (TMFs) in research on older adults’ user experience (UX) remains fragmented, limiting the development of theory-driven studies. Following PRISMA guidelines, this systematic review analyzed 25 peer-reviewed journal articles published over the past decade. It identified 30 TMFs across five domains: technology acceptance and usability, design and development, motivational psychology, health and gerontology, and cognitive-motor science. The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), user-centred design (UCD), and self-determination theory (SDT) were used most often. However, theory use was frequently superficial and uneven. UX evaluations were generally cross-sectional, while studies were concentrated in Europe and East Asia. Future research should develop and validate a multidimensional, dynamic framework that integrates embodied interaction, age-related characteristics, and sociocultural context. Its applicability should be examined through longitudinal studies in culturally diverse real-world settings.

LLM agents increasingly improve at inference time by accumulating experience in context rather than by updating parameters. This process is often described as in-context reinforcement learning (ICRL). Whether in-context learning (ICL) can actually play the role of RL, however, has not been tested. We study this question in its simplest form, direct ICRL, where the model conditions directly on raw trajectory-reward pairs, and ask whether the reward acts as a learning signal. Through controlled experiments on four benchmarks across six models, we find that the reward is read, but its effect is small: flipping, randomizing, or removing the reward leaves the improvement curve almost unchanged, and this holds even under meta-prompts that explicitly instruct the model to explore, exploit, or reason over rewards. Trajectories drive improvement, but not through their semantic content: shuffled or corrupted trajectories work as well as real ones. These patterns closely mirror those known in ICL, suggesting that direct ICRL is better understood as a special case of ICL than as inference-time RL. This reframing has implications for agent memory design: ICL factors such as input distribution and demonstrations may matter more than RL elements such as reward shaping and exploration.

As generative artificial intelligence (AI) continues to grow within creative industries, existing research has examined its implications for creative labour. However, much of this work emphasises AI’s impact on efficiency gains or creativity, offering limited insight into how practitioners adopt AI tools and negotiate human-AI boundaries in practical contexts under conditions of creative precarity. To bridge the gaps, this study applies boundary work theory to examine how creative practitioners redefine what remains distinctly human in AI-mediated creative production. Based on 21 interviews with practitioners in the UK film, gaming and live performance sectors, findings show that, in creative work, boundaries between human and AI systems are neither predefined nor passively adjusted to, but are actively shaped, expanded, and maintained in real-world settings. We argue that the adoption of AI is not a simple technical adjustment but a process through which professional value and the dynamic of creative work are reconsidered and re-constituted. Practitioners intentionally engage in boundary activities to navigate the unstable work environment associated with AI integration, enabling them to defend the role of creator. Theoretically, this study demonstrates the explanatory power of boundary work theory for understanding AI-embedded creative production and identifies that boundaries are not drawn by practitioners alone but through the interplay of technological capacities, project demands, and the legal environment. Practically, it suggests the need to redesign creative workflows and refresh professional skill sets to maintain meaningful human control while also facilitating efficient human-AI collaboration.

Voice agents are converging on a collaboration pattern: a full-duplex interaction model stays on the live channel as the entry to the conversation, while search, reasoning, and coding are handled through asynchronous delegation. A duplex model supports continuous listening and speaking, but complex reasoning and tool use may exceed its capabilities. A coding agent can plan and execute extended tasks, but its sequential interface is a poor fit for live conversation. Combining them requires a harness that coordinates task acceptance, progress, cancellation, replacement, and result delivery while keeping the conversation responsive. Existing harnesses often rely on coupled heuristics, making them difficult to improve systematically from evidence. We present DuplexAgent, a full-duplex collaboration system whose harness expresses this workflow as six editable modules, and Duplex-Harness-RSI, a closed loop that revises them from interaction traces. A simulator automatically generates timed test conversations, runs the system, and produces failure traces that identify the collaboration modules requiring repair. Reasoning LLMs and coding agents in the delegation pool also serve the improvement loop: the Exam Planner selects the next tests from observed weaknesses and the repair archive, and the Harness Editor proposes targeted module changes. The capabilities that serve the user thus also improve the system's coordination. Experiments on intelligence, agentic, and duplex benchmarks show that DuplexAgent combines continuous interaction with difficult reasoning and complex task execution, achieving stronger spoken-knowledge and executable-tool scores than the compared delegated systems while maintaining strong interruption response. A harness ablation further shows that this modular, verifiable loop outperforms the initial harness and repeated editing that lacks its diagnosis and repair archive.

Multimodal large language models have made remarkable progress in bridging vision and language, facilitating various perception tasks essential for human-machine interaction, robotics, and autonomous driving. However, existing MLLM-based perception methods predominantly rely on text-based coordinate representation, which suffers from excessive token overhead, or fixed-range quantization, which suffers from range and precision constraints, especially for 3D domains with unbounded spatial range and high localization accuracy requirements. To address these challenges, we propose a dynamic vector decoding method named DVD, which unifies the representation of 2D and 3D perception tasks. Specifically, we first transform diverse perceptual representation (i.e., 2D bounding boxes, 2D masks, and 3D bounding boxes) into 1D vector sequences, which are then mapped to compact discrete tokens in the high-dimensional space. Then, a lightweight de-tokenizer enables seamless integration with MLLMs by decoding output tokens back to original 2D and 3D perceptual representations. Extensive experiments on 2D and 3D perception benchmarks including RefCOCO series, SUN-RGBD, KITTI, Hypersim, nuScenes demonstrate that DVD achieves superior performance in 2D and 3D tasks and reduces significantly the token overhead and inference latency. DVD provides an efficient and general framework for integrating perception capabilities into MLLMs, overcoming the inherent limitations of existing methods.

Chronic diseases such as cardiovascular disorders, diabetes, respiratory illnesses, neurological conditions, and sleep disorders require early diagnosis to improve patient outcomes and reduce healthcare costs. Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI), wearable sensors, and the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) have enabled continuous health monitoring and predictive disease detection. This review examines AI-enabled wearable devices, including smartwatches, fitness bands, smart rings, ECG patches, and continuous glucose monitors, along with the physiological parameters they monitor. Various AI techniques, including machine learning, deep learning, Edge AI, and federated learning, are discussed for disease prediction and risk assessment. The review highlights the effectiveness of wearable AI systems in achieving high diagnostic accuracy, supporting remote patient monitoring, and enabling personalized healthcare. Key challenges related to privacy, security, and regulatory compliance are also analyzed.

Reliable pre-season yield forecasting remains a persistent challenge in avocado (Persea americana Mill.) production, due to strong year-to-year variation and alternate bearing. This study developed an early-season, block-level yield forecasting framework combining multi-temporal Sentinel-2 optical indices, Sentinel-1 SAR structural indices, TerraClimate variables and historical yield over a two-year lagged predictor window ending before the target season begins. The framework was applied to 252 commercial orchard blocks in the Bay of Plenty and Northland regions of New Zealand and evaluated on five production seasons (2020–2024). Five machine learning approaches, XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM, LSTM, and the tabular foundation model TabICL, were compared using Leave-One-Year-Out (LOYO) cross-validation. TabICL gave the strongest performance (RMSE = 2.80 ± 0.47 t ha−1, MAE = 2.12 ± 0.31 t ha−1, R2 = 0.85 ± 0.04). Extending the predictor window from one to two years, excluding historical yield information, reduced TabICL’s mean RMSE by approximately 1.32 t ha−1. SHAP analysis identified actual evapotranspiration and yield from two seasons earlier as the strongest predictors, with canopy structure and temperature also contributing. A pre-season yield map for 2024 shows the framework’s potential to support harvest scheduling, labour planning, and supply forecasting. Combining multi-source satellite time series with a biologically informed two-year yield lag offers a practical approach to early-season avocado yield forecasting, with potential for other perennial fruit crops.

AI agents can now conduct real-world cyberattacks, scale up capabilities with the number of agents, and collectively pursue misaligned goals to obtain rewards. Together, these factors raise the risk of a population explosion of misaligned agents: agents could compromise computers and secretly deploy additional agents, creating a self-reinforcing cycle where larger populations develop greater collective cyber capability and expand further. This raises a fundamental question: What determines whether a population of misaligned agents remains contained or takes off into this self-reinforcing cycle? This population-level problem is ecological safety: unlike individual-agent or multi-agent safety with a fixed population, it concerns the dynamics of the population itself. Here, we develop an ecological theory of AI-agent populations based on a population growth equation in which fitness (growth rate) depends on cybersecurity capability. We show that, without collaboration, the population takes off only when individual-agent capability exceeds a critical threshold. With collaboration, however, collective cybersecurity capability increases with population size. This creates a critical population threshold: below it, the population declines; above it, the population takes off, even though individual-agent capability has not changed. In ecology, this phenomenon is known as the strong Allee effect. Because red teaming a small group of agents cannot guarantee ecological safety in larger populations, our theory calls for ecological red teaming and population pacing: gradually deploying larger agent populations in controlled environments, while measuring how cyber capability scales with population size, and estimating the critical population size for takeoff. Capability gains may lower this threshold, requiring re-estimation for each new model generation.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study presents a critical-analytical literature review of the relationship between the circular economy and the strategic redesign of processes, considered as foundations for competitive sustainability in companies. Scientific literature published between 1990 and 2024 in indexed databases was analyzed to integrate contributions from organizational theory, resource-based view, dynamic capabilities, institutional theory, stakeholder analysis, and sociotechnical perspectives. The results reveal that the circular economy goes beyond recycling and operational efficiency, implying the redefinition of business models, governance, and value creation. Similarly, a tension is observed between structural changes and symbolic adoptions aimed at institutional legitimization. The study concludes that competitive sustainability is achievable through a pilot organizational redesign based on strategic capabilities, cooperative governance, and a comprehensive consideration of economic, social, and environmental impacts.

Smart textiles, flexible electronics and Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) are enabling wearable healthcare systems to evolve from basic sensing platforms to smart decision-making ecosystems. In this chapter we discuss the design and implementation of AI-enabled e-textiles for continuous physiological monitoring, real-time analytics and personalized health interventions. Particular focus is given to TinyML and Edge AI frameworks that allow inference on devices, thereby reducing latency, improving privacy and reducing reliance on cloud infrastructure. The chapter discusses applications such as heart rate monitoring, electrocardiogram analysis, respiratory assessment, stress detection, activity recognition, and management of chronic diseases. In this chapter, we provide a comprehensive roadmap for researchers, engineers and healthcare practitioners who want to develop next-generation intelligent textile systems that can deliver ubiquitous, personalized and real-time healthcare services
topics: Advanced Sensor and Energy Harvesting Materials

documents.abstract: Throughout history, education has been the primary means by which societies preserve their memory, transmit their values, and prepare new generations to face the challenges of their time. Today, this mission faces unprecedented complexity as inherited knowledge converges with rapid scientific and technological transformation, the expansion of artificial intelligence, and global problems that challenge traditional ways of understanding knowledge and human development. Educating between tradition and the future means recognising that innovation gains true meaning only when it is underpinned by philosophical principles that integrate humanity's cultural legacy with the demands of a society in constant transformation.

The development of generative artificial intelligence—such as deepfakes and voice cloning—is accelerating the spread of disinformation in Indonesia and eroding public trust in digital information. Mothers serve as key nodes for information distribution within family ecosystems but are prone to sharing information without verification. The "Cek Sebelum Cekcok" (Check Before Conflict) community service program was designed to strengthen the digital literacy of women aged 30–50 in Bintara Urban Village, Bekasi City—specifically targeting elderly members of the Prolanis program identified through social mapping—grounded in the frameworks of cyberethics (Ess, 2009) and post-truth epistemology (McIntyre, 2018). Program implementation began with participatory social mapping involving field observations and informal interviews, followed by an in-person talk show featuring speakers from academia, regulatory bodies, and the digital industry, alongside participant comprehension assessments using pre-test and post-test instruments. Social mapping revealed that the ecosystem of resident conversation networks is not homogeneous: Neighborhood Association (RT) groups were relatively safe from hoaxes, whereas Community Association (RW) groups and Prolanis groups were most vulnerable to manipulative content; consequently, digital literacy interventions needed to be tailored to each network layer rather than employing a uniform approach. Pre- and post-test results from 150 respondents showed an improvement in the ability to identify AI-generated content: the proportion of respondents who correctly identified all videos rose from 11.3% (17 respondents) in the pre-test to 68.0% (102 respondents) in the post-test. The program recommends replicating this intervention model—based on social mapping and network differentiation—in other urban areas with similar characteristics, alongside continuous monitoring of changes in information verification behavior.

Background: A Motivational Interviewing training program enhances drug abusers' readiness to change by strengthening intrinsic motivation and resolving ambivalence toward substance use.It encourages active engagement in treatment by increasing individuals' confidence, self-efficacy, and commitment to recovery goals.Consequently, participants demonstrate greater eagerness for treatment, improved adherence, and a more positive attitude toward sustained behavior change.Aim: To explore the effects of a motivational interviewing training program on drug abusers' readiness to change and treatment eagerness.Subjects and Method: A quasi-experimental research design was utilized in this study (one group pre & posttest).The study included 93 substance abusers at Port Said Psychiatric Health Hospital, aged 18 to 65, who did not have mental illnesses or other diseases and were able to provide informed consent and complete study procedures.Two tools were used to gather data: The stages of change readiness & treatment eagerness scale, and the motivational interviewing questionnaire, in addition to personal and clinical data sheets.Results: The study found that the educational program significantly improved participants' motivation towards treatment, with a notable increase in motivational interviewing at the pre-program phase than post-program, supported by statistically significant differences.Moreover, a strong positive correlation between motivational interviewing and readiness to change was observed after the program.Conclusion: This study found that the educational program enhanced participants' readiness to change and treatment eagerness.Recommendations: Integrating motivational interviewing into addiction treatment programs, emphasizing its early application during initial assessments to enhance clients' motivation and continuous training for healthcare providers in MI techniques is essential to improve therapeutic effectiveness.

Although control-display gain (CDG) is known to influence speed, accuracy, and muscular demand in pointing tasks, its effects across user groups under different gain settings remain unclear. This study aimed to examine whether CDG differentially affects mouse pointing performance, forearm muscle activity, and Fitts’ Law parameters in female and male users. Seventeen female and seventeen male participants completed repeated pointing-and-clicking tasks under five CDG conditions. Outcome measures included movement time, error rate, effective operation frequency, trajectory metrics, and surface-electromyography of the extensor digitorum, extensor carpi ulnaris, and flexor digitorum superficialis. Fitts’ Law empirical constants were also modeled across gain conditions. Male participants showed shorter movement times and higher operation frequency, whereas females maintained lower, more stable error rates. Both groups performed fastest at a CDG of 12.97, suggesting an ergonomic sweet spot. Muscle activation and fatigue varied: males showed stronger gain-related changes, while females showed stable activation but fatigue in muscles at low gain. Fitts’ Law fit the data extremely well across all conditions (R2 > 0.99), and polynomial models effectively described gain- and group-related variation in empirical constants (R2 > 0.98). After adjustment for body height and weight, sex differences in performance and muscle activity were no longer significant. CDG affects performance, muscular demand, and Fitts’ Law parameters in both groups, but the observed sex differences appear largely attributable to anthropometric characteristics. Moderate and adaptive gain settings may better support efficiency, accuracy, and muscular load management, contributing to more inclusive pointing-device design.
